title: The groupthink trap
performance: in their next decision meeting, the viewer notices when silence is being taken as agreement and uses one habit (the leader speaks last, everyone writes a view first, a named critic, or a premortem) to get the unspoken doubts said before the team commits

audience.assumed_prior: has sat in many decision meetings and has nodded along while privately unsure; probably has no name for the pattern and no habit to stop it
audience.why: the brief's audience runs or sits in decision meetings; the skill is judgement in a familiar situation, not new theory
audience.motivation: part of a corporate learning programme; mildly sceptical of meeting advice, cares about not owning an avoidable mistake and not looking difficult
audience.context: desk or laptop, with sound, captions on; a short watch between meetings

strategy.name: scenario_led
strategy.rationale: the knowledge sheet is a mechanism (F3, F6, F9) plus remedies (F11, F12, F14, F15); for practitioners that teaches best as one meeting shown going wrong, then the same meeting replayed with the remedies, so consequences carry the judgement
strategy.signature_move: show the team at one decision moment, let the viewer see the hidden doubt, show what happens next, THEN name the pattern or habit in one plain sentence

misconceptions.why_tempting: a quiet room after 'any objections?' looks and feels like consent, and moving on saves time
misconceptions.source_anchor: knowledge F6 (self-censorship, illusion of unanimity), F9 (pluralistic ignorance)
misconceptions.refutation: the viewer sees every member's private doubt while the hands go up one by one; the vote looks unanimous and the thoughts say otherwise; then the narrator says it plainly: the silence was not agreement

misconceptions.belief: groupthink happens to weaker teams; a smart team would catch it
misconceptions.why_tempting: bad decisions feel like a competence problem, and capable people trust their own judgement
misconceptions.source_anchor: knowledge F4 (the drive to agree, not a lack of intelligence; Janis's capable decision makers), F3
misconceptions.refutation: the team is shown as capable and reasonable, each doubt is a good one, and the failure comes anyway; the narrator names F4's point in one line: the cause is the drive to agree, not the people

misconceptions.belief: the fix is braver people who just speak up
misconceptions.why_tempting: it is what we tell ourselves afterwards, and it puts the fix inside each person rather than in how the meeting runs
misconceptions.source_anchor: brief through_line; knowledge F16 (people expect speaking up to be pointless or costly), F11, F14, F15
misconceptions.refutation: the replay keeps the same people with the same nerves; nobody becomes braver, yet every doubt reaches the table because each habit makes saying it the expected move; the narrator says so in one sentence

hook.sketch: Say five smart people meet to decide one plan, and every one of them privately doubts it. The plan passes with every hand up.

arc.promise: by the end you have four habits that get those doubts said before your next team commits
arc.bridge_from_prior: sec1 opens from the meeting the viewer has sat in: the moment they nodded along while unsure, and assumed they were the only one

sections.title: The meeting that agreed
sections.goal: the viewer can explain how a capable team ends up agreeing to a plan most of its members privately doubt
sections.carrier: scenario: one meeting room, five people round one table; the leader says what she wants first, one colleague agrees fast, and each other person's doubt appears as a private thought only the viewer can see; hands go up one at a time until the vote looks total; time steps forward and the plan fails on exactly those doubts
sections.recap: the leader spoke first, everyone else kept their doubt, and the silence looked like a yes
sections.teaching_notes: open with 'say' to frame the team as invented; the leader is reasonable, not a villain; refute misconceptions 1 and 2 here; name groupthink only AFTER the failure, with F1 (Janis developed the idea studying capable decision makers) and F3 in plain words; never say Janis coined the word (F2); slowdown on 'each one thinks they are the only doubter'; carry F17 in one plain line (a useful description with mixed evidence, not a law); F5, F7 and F10 are not voiced here

sections.title: Same meeting, four habits
sections.goal: the viewer can use four habits to bring hidden doubts out before a decision: the leader speaks last, everyone writes a view first, one person is the named critic, and the team runs a premortem
sections.carrier: replay: the same room and the same people, rewound; each habit turns one of the private thoughts from sec1 face up as a written note on the table, so the notes pile up where the empty agreement was; the plan gets changed before it ships
sections.recap: nobody got braver; the meeting made the doubt the expected thing to say
sections.teaching_notes: worked example: narrate each habit as it lands on one specific doubt the viewer already saw; refute misconception 3 at the end; per F12's caveat, the critic's job is to make real doubts easier to say, not to stage fake ones; per F15's caveat, attach no measured improvement to the premortem; never say a habit guarantees a good decision; four terms is this section's limit, so no other new words

sections.title: Your next meeting
sections.goal: the viewer can use the right habit when a meeting goes quiet after the leader has already said what she wants
concepts: choosing a habit in the moment
sections.carrier: a fresh moment in the same team's next meeting, frozen at the quiet after 'so, we're all agreed?'; the four habits sit beside it as a short set the viewer picks from; then the reveal, and the team back at the table, changed
sections.teaching_notes: faded practice through the one quiz; F10 may be voiced in one line as the reason the answer works (one other voice makes it easier for the rest), without numbers and with its laboratory caveat kept implicit by saying 'can'; end by returning to the team, changed

arc.payoff: Back at the first team's table, the doubts that sank the plan now sit on it, written and said; the viewer names the habit they will use in their next meeting.

practice_ladder.what: the replayed meeting, each habit narrated as it brings out one doubt
a new quiet moment; the viewer picks the habit before the team shows it
the viewer picks one habit for a real meeting on their own calendar

slowdown_at: each doubter thinks they are the only one

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Keep those four private doubts in mind; we are about to rewind the meeting.
Next meeting. The leader has already said what she wants, asks 'any objections?', and the room goes quiet. Which habit do you reach for now?
recall_moments.answer: ask everyone to write down, on their own, one reason the plan could fail, then read them out; it brings each doubt out without anyone having to go first
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: 'take the quiet as a yes, or ask for objections again': silence is not agreement, and asking out loud asks each doubter to be the first and only one to object, which is exactly what they expect to cost them

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Remember the first meeting: every doubt was there all along; it just had nowhere to go.

transfer_tasks: pick one decision on your calendar this week and choose one of the four habits for it before the meeting starts
if you run the meeting, say your own view last

persona.voice: the storyteller: warm, close, a colleague telling a story about a meeting everyone has sat in, a little wry
persona.delivery_notes: present tense and unhurried for the story; a beat of silence after the hands go up and before the plain lesson; slower on the slowdown line; brisk and light on the four habits; warm and settled at the close, never cheerleading

gagne.attention: hook: five doubts, five hands up
gagne.objective: promise: four habits before your next team commits
gagne.recall_prior: sec1 bridges from the viewer nodding along while unsure
gagne.present: sec1 mechanism shown in one meeting, sec2 habits in the replay
gagne.guidance: signature move plus the worked replay in sec2
gagne.practice: the quiz after sec2; practice ladder
gagne.feedback: quiz answer explains why writing first works and why asking again out loud fails
gagne.assess: the quiz is the single check; payoff asks the viewer to name their habit
gagne.transfer: transfer tasks: one habit on a real meeting this week; speak last if you lead

merrill.problem_centered: one team's one decision runs through every section
merrill.activation: sec1 bridge from the viewer's own nodding-along moment
merrill.demonstration: sec2 replays the same meeting with each habit working on a doubt we saw
merrill.application: sec3 quiz makes the viewer choose the habit before the reveal
merrill.integration: payoff and transfer tasks put a habit on the viewer's own calendar

mayer.coherence: one team, one meeting, one plan; no history lesson, no second scenario
mayer.signalling: one slowdown, on the only-doubter line
mayer.redundancy: screen shows the hidden thoughts, the notes and the four habit names; the voice tells the story
mayer.contiguity: each doubt appears on the person who holds it, each note lands as its habit is named
mayer.segmenting: three short sections, one job each
mayer.pre_training: sec1 shows the pieces (the leader's view, private doubts, silent hands) before sec2 names habits that act on them

arcs.attention: the visible private doubts against the unanimous hands
arcs.relevance: the viewer's own decision meetings this week
arcs.confidence: a fully worked replay before the one question
arcs.satisfaction: the first team's doubts end up on the table, and the viewer leaves with one habit chosen
